effect_on_phenotype: Converts CYP2D6 NM/IM to phenotypic PM. Paroxetine is a mechanism-based (irreversible) inhibitor that effectively abolishes CYP2D6 activity regardless of genotype.
clinical_significance: Critically important during tamoxifen therapy — co-administration reduces endoxifen levels by 50-65%, potentially reducing breast cancer treatment efficacy. Co-prescription should be avoided.
affected_substrate_drugs: tamoxifen, codeine, tramadol, atomoxetine, metoprolol, ondansetron, venlafaxine, dextromethorphan
reversibility: Irreversible (mechanism-based inhibitor); recovery requires new enzyme synthesis, approximately 2 weeks after paroxetine discontinuation
text_chunk: Paroxetine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Paroxetine is a potent mechanism-based inhibitor of CYP2D6, forming a quasi-irreversible metabolite-intermediate complex. This converts any CYP2D6 genotypic phenotype to a functional poor metabolizer. The clinical impact is most significant for tamoxifen — Kelly et al. (BMJ 2010) showed increased breast cancer mortality when paroxetine was co-prescribed with tamoxifen. ASCO guidelines recommend avoiding strong CYP2D6 inhibitors during tamoxifen therapy.

effect_on_phenotype: Converts CYP2D6 NM/IM to phenotypic PM. Both fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine are potent CYP2D6 inhibitors.
clinical_significance: Long half-life of norfluoxetine (4-16 days) means phenoconversion persists weeks after fluoxetine discontinuation. Affects all CYP2D6 substrates including codeine, tamoxifen.
affected_substrate_drugs: tamoxifen, codeine, tramadol, atomoxetine, metoprolol, ondansetron
time_to_onset: 7-14 days to full inhibition (due to long half-life)
reversibility: Reversible but very slow; allow 5-6 weeks washout (5x norfluoxetine half-life) before substrate drug initiation
text_chunk: Fluoxetine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Fluoxetine and its long-lived active metabolite norfluoxetine (t1/2 4-16 days) are potent competitive CYP2D6 inhibitors. The prolonged inhibition window is unique among SSRIs. When switching from fluoxetine to a CYP2D6 substrate, a 5-6 week washout is recommended. This is particularly relevant when switching antidepressants or initiating codeine/tramadol therapy.

effect_on_phenotype: Converts CYP2D6 NM to phenotypic PM. Bupropion and its metabolite hydroxybupropion are potent CYP2D6 inhibitors.
clinical_significance: Affects co-administered CYP2D6 substrates. Important when bupropion is used for smoking cessation alongside codeine-containing analgesics or with tamoxifen.
affected_substrate_drugs: codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen, metoprolol, atomoxetine, dextromethorphan
reversibility: Reversible; recovery within 5-7 days after bupropion discontinuation
text_chunk: Bupropion-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Bupropion is classified as a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor by the FDA. Hydroxybupropion (active metabolite) contributes to the inhibitory effect. In vivo, bupropion increases dextromethorphan AUC 5-6 fold, consistent with strong inhibition. This is often overlooked since bupropion is not primarily an antidepressant in many patients' minds.

effect_on_phenotype: Converts CYP2D6 NM to phenotypic PM. Quinidine is the most potent known CYP2D6 inhibitor (Ki ~50 nM).
clinical_significance: Used therapeutically in combination with dextromethorphan (Nuedexta) to deliberately inhibit CYP2D6. At sub-antiarrhythmic doses, quinidine effectively phenocopies CYP2D6 PM status.
affected_substrate_drugs: dextromethorphan, codeine, tramadol, all CYP2D6 substrates
reversibility: Reversible; competitive inhibitor with short half-life (6-8 hours); recovery within 1-2 days
text_chunk: Quinidine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Quinidine is the prototypical strong CYP2D6 inhibitor used as the positive control in CYP2D6 phenotyping studies. Its potency (Ki ~50 nM) means even low doses effectively abolish CYP2D6 activity. The combination dextromethorphan/quinidine (Nuedexta) exploits this interaction therapeutically for pseudobulbar affect treatment.

effect_on_phenotype: Converts CYP2D6 NM to phenotypic PM. Terbinafine is a mechanism-based inhibitor with prolonged effect duration.
clinical_significance: Often overlooked as a CYP2D6 inhibitor since it is an antifungal. Important during chronic onychomycosis treatment (3-6 months) when patients are also on CYP2D6 substrates.
reversibility: Very slow recovery due to mechanism-based inhibition and long tissue half-life (200-400 hours); may persist 4-6 weeks after discontinuation
text_chunk: Terbinafine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Terbinafine is a frequently overlooked potent CYP2D6 inhibitor. It forms a reactive metabolite that inactivates CYP2D6 (mechanism-based inhibition). The extremely long tissue half-life means inhibitory effects can persist for weeks after treatment completion. Clinicians should be aware of this interaction during the months-long courses used for onychomycosis.

effect_on_phenotype: Partially inhibits CYP2D6; converts NM to approximate IM phenotype. Less potent than paroxetine or fluoxetine.
clinical_significance: Moderate clinical relevance. May increase exposure to CYP2D6 substrates by 50-100%.
text_chunk: Duloxetine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Duloxetine is classified as a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor. It increases dextromethorphan AUC approximately 2.5-fold. The clinical significance is intermediate — may not fully convert NMs to PMs but can push IMs to phenotypic PM status.

effect_on_phenotype: Potently inhibits CYP1A2 activity. Converts CYP1A2 rapid metabolizer (smoker) phenotype to effective PM status.
clinical_significance: Critical for clozapine and olanzapine dosing. Co-administration with clozapine can increase clozapine levels 5-10 fold, risking seizures and cardiac toxicity.
affected_substrate_drugs: clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline, caffeine, tizanidine, duloxetine
reversibility: Reversible; recovery within 3-5 days after fluvoxamine discontinuation
text_chunk: Fluvoxamine-CYP1A2 phenoconversion: Fluvoxamine is the most potent CYP1A2 inhibitor among SSRIs. The interaction with clozapine is potentially life-threatening — case reports document clozapine levels increasing from therapeutic (300-600 ng/mL) to toxic (>1000 ng/mL) upon fluvoxamine addition. Conversely, fluvoxamine is sometimes deliberately used at low doses to boost clozapine levels in rapid metabolizers (smokers).

effect_on_phenotype: Potently inhibits CYP1A2. Can dramatically increase levels of CYP1A2 substrates.
clinical_significance: Dangerous with theophylline (seizure risk) and tizanidine (severe hypotension). Tizanidine is contraindicated with ciprofloxacin.
reversibility: Reversible; competitive inhibitor; recovery within 2-3 days
text_chunk: Ciprofloxacin-CYP1A2 phenoconversion: Ciprofloxacin is a potent CYP1A2 inhibitor that increases tizanidine AUC 10-fold and theophylline AUC 2-3 fold. The FDA label for tizanidine lists ciprofloxacin co-administration as contraindicated. Clinicians prescribing short-course ciprofloxacin must check for CYP1A2 substrate interactions.

effect_on_phenotype: Potent CYP3A4 (and CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2B6) inducer via PXR activation. Converts any CYP3A4 phenotype to ultra-rapid metabolizer status.
clinical_significance: Reduces exposure to virtually all CYP3A4 substrates by 50-90%. Critical for immunosuppressants (tacrolimus levels become undetectable), oral contraceptives (failure), and many antiretrovirals.
affected_substrate_drugs: tacrolimus, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, midazolam, simvastatin, imatinib, voriconazole, warfarin
time_to_onset: 3-7 days for full induction; maximal at 7-10 days
reversibility: Reversible; de-induction requires 2 weeks (CYP3A4 half-life ~36 hours; 5 half-lives for return to baseline)
text_chunk: Rifampin-CYP3A4 phenoconversion (induction): Rifampin is the most potent clinically relevant CYP inducer, activating the pregnane X receptor (PXR/NR1I2). It upregulates CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2B6, UGT, and P-glycoprotein expression. Tacrolimus dose requirements may increase 5-10 fold during rifampin co-administration. This drug-drug-gene interaction is critical because even CYP3A5 non-expressers become ultra-rapid CYP3A metabolizers.

effect_on_phenotype: Strong CYP3A4 inducer. Also induces CYP2C9, CYP2C19, UGTs, and P-glycoprotein. Auto-induces its own metabolism.
clinical_significance: Reduces exposure to hormonal contraceptives, immunosuppressants, and many other CYP3A4 substrates. Auto-induction causes carbamazepine levels to decline over first 2-4 weeks.
affected_substrate_drugs: oral contraceptives, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, simvastatin, midazolam, quetiapine, aripiprazole, warfarin
reversibility: Reversible; de-induction over 2-3 weeks after discontinuation
text_chunk: Carbamazepine-CYP3A4 induction phenoconversion: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 via constitutive androstane receptor (CAR/NR1I3) and PXR. It also auto-induces its own metabolism (CYP3A4-mediated), requiring dose escalation over the first 2-4 weeks. The induction effect on hormonal contraceptives is particularly important — breakthrough ovulation and unintended pregnancy can occur.

effect_on_phenotype: Potent CYP3A4 competitive inhibitor. Effectively converts any CYP3A4 phenotype to poor metabolizer status.
clinical_significance: Dramatically increases exposure to CYP3A4 substrates. Used as the FDA-recommended strong CYP3A4 inhibitor for drug interaction studies. Systemic ketoconazole withdrawn in many countries.
affected_substrate_drugs: midazolam, simvastatin, lovastatin, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, sirolimus
reversibility: Reversible; competitive inhibitor; recovery within 3-5 days
text_chunk: Ketoconazole-CYP3A4 phenoconversion (inhibition): Ketoconazole is the prototypical strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, used as the standard positive control in regulatory drug interaction studies. Systemic oral ketoconazole has been withdrawn or restricted in many countries due to hepatotoxicity risk, but the DDI principle applies to other azole antifungals (itraconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole) with varying potency.

effect_on_phenotype: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. Itraconazole and its active metabolite hydroxyitraconazole both inhibit CYP3A4.
clinical_significance: Increases midazolam AUC 6-10 fold. Contraindicated with many CYP3A4 substrates including simvastatin, lovastatin, pimozide, and certain immunosuppressants without dose adjustment.
affected_substrate_drugs: simvastatin, lovastatin, midazolam, triazolam, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, ibrutinib, venetoclax
reversibility: Slow reversal due to long half-life of hydroxyitraconazole (20-30 hours); recovery 5-7 days
text_chunk: Itraconazole-CYP3A4 phenoconversion: Itraconazole is classified as a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. Both parent drug and the active metabolite hydroxyitraconazole contribute to inhibition. The prolonged half-life means inhibitory effects persist for days after discontinuation. The interaction with ibrutinib and venetoclax is particularly relevant in oncology, where dose reductions or avoidance are required.

effect_on_phenotype: Potent CYP2C9 inhibitor and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor at doses >=200mg. Converts CYP2C9 NM to phenotypic PM.
clinical_significance: Dramatically increases warfarin sensitivity and INR. Co-administration requires 25-50% warfarin dose reduction and frequent INR monitoring. Also affects phenytoin and celecoxib levels.
reversibility: Reversible; recovery within 5-7 days due to long fluconazole half-life (30 hours)
text_chunk: Fluconazole-CYP2C9 phenoconversion: Fluconazole is a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor, particularly relevant for warfarin-treated patients. Even short courses of fluconazole (e.g., for vulvovaginal candidiasis) can cause dangerous INR elevation in warfarin patients. This represents a drug-drug-gene interaction: CYP2C9 IMs on warfarin are particularly vulnerable because fluconazole converts their remaining CYP2C9 activity to near-zero.

effect_on_phenotype: Moderate inhibitor of multiple CYPs including CYP2D6, CYP1A2, CYP3A4. Partially reduces CYP2D6 activity.
clinical_significance: Generally less clinically significant than strong CYP2D6 inhibitors. May contribute to drug interactions when combined with other moderate inhibitors.
reversibility: Reversible; competitive inhibitor; recovery within 1-2 days
text_chunk: Cimetidine-CYP2D6 phenoconversion: Cimetidine is a non-selective inhibitor of multiple CYP enzymes including CYP2D6 (moderate), CYP1A2 (weak-moderate), and CYP3A4 (weak). Its clinical significance has diminished with the widespread use of PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists with fewer DDI (ranitidine, famotidine). However, it remains relevant as a textbook example of broad CYP inhibition.

effect_on_phenotype: Moderate inhibitor of CYP2C9 (and weak CYP2D6 inhibitor). Increases warfarin sensitivity substantially due to CYP2C9 inhibition and independent anticoagulant effect.
clinical_significance: Warfarin dose should be reduced by 30-50% when amiodarone is initiated. Effect persists months after amiodarone discontinuation due to extremely long half-life (40-55 days).
reversibility: Extremely slow reversal due to amiodarone half-life of 40-55 days; effects may persist 2-3 months after discontinuation
text_chunk: Amiodarone-CYP2C9 phenoconversion: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and P-glycoprotein. The warfarin interaction is clinically critical and included in the IWPC pharmacogenomic warfarin dosing algorithm as a covariate. The extremely long half-life (40-55 days) means that amiodarone's inhibitory effect persists for months after discontinuation. Amiodarone use status is a standard question in warfarin dose prediction models.

effect_on_phenotype: Strong CYP1A2 inducer. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (not nicotine) in tobacco smoke activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), inducing CYP1A2 expression 2-4 fold.
clinical_significance: Smokers require substantially higher doses of clozapine, olanzapine, and theophylline. Smoking cessation causes rapid loss of induction with dangerous rise in drug levels.
affected_substrate_drugs: clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline, caffeine, fluvoxamine, duloxetine
time_to_onset: Chronic induction; maintained during ongoing smoking
reversibility: Reversible upon smoking cessation; de-induction occurs over 3-7 days. Clozapine dose must be reduced 30-40% upon smoking cessation.
text_chunk: Smoking-CYP1A2 induction phenoconversion: Tobacco smoking (via PAH-mediated AhR activation) induces CYP1A2 2-4 fold. This is clinically critical for clozapine-treated patients: smokers require ~50% higher clozapine doses. Hospitalization-related smoking cessation is a known precipitant of clozapine toxicity (NMS, seizures) due to rapid de-induction. NRT patches do not maintain induction because nicotine is not the inducer.

effect_on_phenotype: Strong CYP3A4 inducer via PXR activation by hyperforin. Also induces CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and P-glycoprotein.
clinical_significance: Reduces oral contraceptive efficacy (breakthrough bleeding/pregnancy), reduces cyclosporine and tacrolimus levels (graft rejection), and reduces antiretroviral efficacy.
affected_substrate_drugs: oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, indinavir, irinotecan, warfarin, simvastatin
reversibility: Reversible; de-induction over 1-2 weeks after discontinuation
text_chunk: St. John's Wort-CYP3A4 induction phenoconversion: Hyperforin, the active component, is a potent PXR agonist that induces CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, UGT, and P-glycoprotein. Multiple case reports document transplant rejection (cyclosporine), oral contraceptive failure, and serotonin syndrome (when combined with SSRIs). This is the most clinically significant herbal-drug interaction and is often not disclosed by patients.

effect_on_phenotype: Irreversible inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4 by furanocoumarins (bergamottin, 6',7'-dihydroxybergamottin). Hepatic CYP3A4 is not affected at typical consumption levels.
clinical_significance: Increases oral bioavailability of CYP3A4 substrates with high first-pass metabolism. Effects are intestinal only, so IV-administered drugs are not affected.
affected_substrate_drugs: simvastatin, lovastatin, felodipine, cyclosporine, buspirone, midazolam (oral)
reversibility: Irreversible (mechanism-based); intestinal CYP3A4 recovery requires new enzyme synthesis over 24-72 hours
text_chunk: Grapefruit-CYP3A4 phenoconversion: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit form reactive epoxide intermediates that irreversibly inactivate intestinal CYP3A4. A single glass of grapefruit juice can reduce intestinal CYP3A4 activity by >50%. The effect is most pronounced for drugs with high first-pass metabolism (felodipine AUC increases 2-3 fold, simvastatin up to 16-fold). Seville oranges and pomelos contain similar furanocoumarins.
